newsitem.title: UK: UK gas Network Code "needs modification" - Eastern.
newsitem.headline: UK gas Network Code "needs modification" - Eastern.

text.p: The Network Code, the "rulebook" which governs natural gas trade in Britain by regulating use of the trunk pipeline system, is not working as it was intended and needs modification, a senior industry official said on Thursday.

Bob Bruce, transportation and regulation manager of Eastern Natural Gas, part of Hanson Plc, said British Gas Plc unit TransCo, operator of the pipeline network, was retaining too much control over trading activity.
"TransCo must cease restricting trading activity, it must accept that markets must be unrestricted and that they will then deliver gas," he told a conference.
Bruce said TransCo fears markets will not deliver gas as required, which leads it to believe it needs to maintain close control of the transport system.

This in turn restricts trading under the Network Code, which means that trade on the flexibility mechanism, designed to provide liquidity and transparency on the market, remains illiquid and disrupts the spot market, Bruce said.
With spot market trade hindered, Bruce said, TransCo's fear that the market cannot deliver is legitimised, and the whole vicious circle starts again.
The Network Code was introduced in two phases, known as the soft and hard landings, in March and September.

It has three aims, according to Bruce: to allow gas shippers and TransCo to fulfil statutory obligations, to set down "sustainable commercial arrangements" and to avoid undue influence on the wider gas industry.

In particular, shippers are now obliged to balance inputs and offtakes of gas into the trunk pipeline network, the National Transmission System (NTS), daily. Failure to do so incurs a financial penalty.
But Bruce believes the Network Code can only work if it allows markets to work.
"We didn't have clear expectations of the Network Code except that it had to be there and it had to work," he said.
But this is not now happening, Bruce said.
"TransCo is missing an opportunity to get people to meet the requirements of the system by combined efforts, not individual efforts."

There are several aspects of the code which are particularly harmful, Bruce said. The underlying problem was that separating shipper incentives by penalising shippers for imbalances did not deliver system requirements.

The penal regime for being out of balance exposes shippers to large risks, but these are not related to individual shipper actions but are "smearable" across the industry, Bruce said. And with variable costs, charges are impossible to predict.
But Bruce also said TransCo had been forced to come to terms with the new trading regime extremely quickly.

"There have been fundamental changes in the structure of the U.K. market, especially as far as British Gas is concerned. A major company, TransCo, has been brought into being as operator of the new system, and the effort involved in this should not be underestimated."
Another speaker at the conference, Lynn Johansen of law firm Clifford Chance, echoed some of Bruce's concerns. "The Network Code will need more revision," she said.
She warned that trade at the National Balancing Point (NBP), which is becoming increasingly common on the spot market, could present problems.

"...the NBP is not once mentioned in the Network Code. Its provisions are not very clear and they don't match up with what the system ought to do. We need to look at the Netwrok Code closely and ask questions."
--Sebastian Alison, London Newsroom, +44 171 542 6412
